Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chinese hackers target telcos with new Linux, Windows malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] JFMBackdoor DLL sideload via fltMC.exe executed outside System32 · [LLM] Showboat Linux implant masquerading as kernel kworker thread · [LLM] Calypso JFMBackdoor known SHA256 file or process execution · Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Showboat dead-drop C2 fetch from Pastebin or paste services · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] JFMBackdoor DLL sideload via fltMC.exe executed outside System32 Installation High
Detects Calypso/Red Lamassu's JFMBackdoor stage where the batch loader drops fltMC.exe alongside a malicious FLTLIB.dll into a writable directory and launches the legitimate Microsoft Filter Manager Control binary to sideload the trojanised DLL. The signal is fltMC.exe execution from any path other than %WinDir%\System32 or %WinDir%\SysWOW64. Rationale: PwC's reported infection chain explicitly names fltMC.exe + FLTLIB.dll as the JFMBackdoor sideloading pair. Legitimate fltMC.exe only ships in System32/SysWOW64; any other execution path is high-fidelity evidence of staged sideload. HijackLibs.net independently catalogues fltlib.dll as a confirmed sideloading target for fltMC.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://hijacklibs.net/entries/microsoft/built-in/fltlib.html • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/chinese-group-calypso-exploiting-microsoft-exchange • https://therecord.media/suspected-chinese-state-linked-threat-actors-infiltrated-major-afghan-telecom-provider
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Image_Load
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let SideloadedFltMc = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName =~ "fltMC.exe"
    | where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\"
       and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\"
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessId,
              FltMcPath = FolderPath, FltMcCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
              ParentName = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              ParentCmd  = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256;
SideloadedFltMc
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName =~ "FLTLIB.dll"
    | where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\"
       and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\"
    | project DeviceId, LoaderProcessId = InitiatingProcessId,
              FltLibPath = FolderPath, FltLibSha256 = SHA256
  ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FltMcPath, FltMcCmd,
          ParentName, ParentCmd, ParentPath,
          FltLibPath, FltLibSha256, FltMcSha256 = SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\fltMC.exe"
| where not (NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\" or NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Showboat Linux implant masquerading as kernel kworker thread Installation High
Detects user-space Linux processes that mimic the kernel kworker naming convention used by Calypso's Showboat implant. Genuine kworker entries are kernel threads with no on-disk executable and are children of kthreadd (PID 2); any process_create event whose image name begins with 'kworker' AND has a real executable path is the implant. Rationale: Black Lotus Labs explicitly names the Showboat implant variant as 'Showboat/kworker', meaning the implant adopts the kworker process name. Kernel kworker threads are emitted by the scheduler and have no on-disk executable; any process_create event with a kworker-prefixed image name AND a real path is almost certainly the implant. The PID-2 (kthreadd) parent filter further excludes any rare scheduler-related noise. Cross-checked against: • https://news.drweb.com/show/?i=14451 • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/chinese-apt-groups-target-afghan-telecommunications-firm
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let LinuxHosts = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OSPlatform =~ "Linux"
    | distinct DeviceId;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DeviceId in (LinuxHosts)
| where FileName startswith "kworker" or ProcessCommandLine startswith "kworker"
| where isnotempty(FolderPath) and FolderPath !startswith "/proc/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentName = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentId   = InitiatingProcessId,
          ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd  = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DvcOs has "Linux"
| where TargetProcessName startswith "kworker" or ActingProcessName startswith "kworker"
| where ParentProcessId != 2     // genuine kworker is a child of kthreadd (PID 2)
| where isnotempty(TargetProcessName)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessId,
          TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Showboat dead-drop C2 fetch from Pastebin or paste services Command & Control Medium
Detects the Showboat 'hide' command's dead-drop retrieval where the implant fetches the next-stage code from Pastebin or similar public paste services. Signal is HTTP/DNS from non-browser, non-developer-tooling processes (typically the kworker-masquerading implant) to known paste sites — a behaviour that should be near-zero on telco production hosts. Rationale: Black Lotus Labs explicitly documents that Showboat's 'hide' command uses Pastebin and online forums as a dead-drop resolver — the in-article screenshot 'Pastebin page used in the attacks' anchors this behaviour. A non-browser process hitting Pastebin on a telco production server has near-zero benign baseline. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/u/1220909/2026/May/pastebit.jpg • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/001/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let PasteHosts = dynamic(["pastebin.com","rentry.co","paste.ee","ghostbin.com","hastebin.com","0bin.net","controlc.com","justpaste.it","dpaste.com"]);
let Browsers = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe","safari.exe","vivaldi.exe","firefox","chromium","chrome"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Host = tolower(tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host))
| where Host has_any (PasteHosts) or RemoteUrl has_any (PasteHosts)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (Browsers)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let PasteHosts = dynamic(["pastebin.com","rentry.co","paste.ee","ghostbin.com","hastebin.com","0bin.net","controlc.com","justpaste.it","dpaste.com"]);
let Browsers = dynamic(["Chrome","Firefox","Edge","Safari","Brave","Opera","Vivaldi"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| extend HostName = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Url).Host))
| where HostName has_any (PasteHosts)
| where not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any (Browsers))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, Url,
          HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr,
          DstPortNumber, HttpMethod
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Browser Process Contacting Paste-Site Dead Drop (Showboat C2)

[LLM] Calypso JFMBackdoor known SHA256 file or process execution Installation High
Hash-based IOC detection for the JFMBackdoor sample reported in the Black Lotus Labs / PwC Calypso campaign write-up. Fires on any file write or process execution matching the SHA256 d6a4fad5448838dbc8cc6b33f1dbfbdc7a2fad36de58ff6a66dce96f729f7011 across endpoint telemetry. Rationale: The article (Black Lotus Labs / PwC primary source) publishes the SHA256 d6a4fad5448838dbc8cc6b33f1dbfbdc7a2fad36de58ff6a66dce96f729f7011 as the reported Calypso sample. Hash-IOC detections have effectively zero false-positive rate at SHA256 length and provide a precise tripwire for the exact JFMBackdoor binary in use during this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-target-telcos-with-new-linux-windows-malware/
ATT&CKT1219 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
let BadHash = "d6a4fad5448838dbc8cc6b33f1dbfbdc7a2fad36de58ff6a66dce96f729f7011";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 == BadHash
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="FileEvent"),
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 == BadHash or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == BadHash
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
              ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="ProcessEvent"),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 == BadHash
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImageLoad")
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadHash = "d6a4fad5448838dbc8cc6b33f1dbfbdc7a2fad36de58ff6a66dce96f729f7011";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFileSHA256 =~ BadHash or Hash =~ BadHash
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath,
              TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, Source="ImFileEvent"),
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where FileHash has BadHash
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName,
              CommandLine, FileHash, Source="4688"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where FileHash =~ BadHash
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, FileName, FileHash,
              SourceIP, DestinationIP, Source="CSL")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Service Persistence via sc.exe with User-Writable Path
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0e
status: experimental
description: |
    sc.exe create with the binary path under \Users\, \AppData\,
    \ProgramData\, or \Temp\ — service-install persistence outside
    legitimate program directories.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1543.003
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_sc:
        Image|endswith: '\sc.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: 'create'

        CommandLine|contains:
            - '\Users\'
            - '\AppData\'
            - '\ProgramData\'
            - '\Temp\'

falsepositives:

level: high

[LLM] Vulnerable Cisco Secure Workload version present in asset fleet (CVE-2026-20223) Reconnaissance High
Surfaces hosts/appliances in the asset inventory running Cisco Secure Workload (formerly Tetration) at versions below the fixed releases 3.10.8.3 / 4.0.3.17. Exploit grants unauthenticated Site Admin on internal REST APIs (CVSS 10.0), so this is a pre-exploit deploy-blocker hunt — patch confirmation rather than behavioural detection. Rationale: Article gives the exact fixed-release pivots (3.10.8.3, 4.0.3.17) and the affected version bands (3.9-and-earlier must migrate, all 3.10 lines and all 4.0 lines below the fixed minors). Joined Defender TVM to Software Inventory so the output names the appliance + version + recommended target release — actionable patch-list rather than a CVE-id list. Cross-checked Cisco PSIRT (no in-the-wild exploitation reported), securityonline.info (CVSS 10.0, internal REST APIs only, web mgmt UI unaffected), and cybersecuritynews.com (no PoC / no public IOCs at disclosure). Cross-checked against: • https://securityonline.info/cisco-secure-workload-api-vulnerability-cve-2026-20223-cvess-10/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cisco-secure-workload-vulnerability/ • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/05/21/cisco-serves-up-yet-another-perfect-10-bug-with-secure-workload-admin-flaw/5244012 • https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-20223
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-20223"
    or (SoftwareVendor =~ "cisco" and (SoftwareName has_any ("secure workload","tetration")))
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where SoftwareVendor =~ "cisco" and SoftwareName has_any ("secure workload","tetration")
    | project DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
  ) on DeviceId
| extend NeedsPatch = case(
    SoftwareVersion startswith "3.9" or SoftwareVersion startswith "3.8" or SoftwareVersion startswith "3.7", "migrate-off-3.9-and-earlier",
    SoftwareVersion startswith "3.10" and SoftwareVersion != "3.10.8.3" and not(SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^3\.10\.([89]|1[0-9])\."), "upgrade-to-3.10.8.3",
    SoftwareVersion startswith "4.0" and SoftwareVersion != "4.0.3.17" and not(SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^4\.0\.([4-9]|1[0-9])\."), "upgrade-to-4.0.3.17",
    "verify-version"
  )
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, NeedsPatch
| order by DeviceName asc

[LLM] Cisco Secure Workload Site Admin action crossing tenant boundary in a single session Exploitation Medium
Hunts the defining behavioral signature of CVE-2026-20223: the exploit grants unauthenticated Site Admin and lets the attacker make configuration changes ACROSS tenant boundaries. Legitimate Site Admin sessions are normally scoped to one tenant at a time, so a single principal/source touching two or more distinct tenant scopes within a short window is the high-fidelity pivot. Requires Secure Workload audit logs forwarded via syslog/CEF to Sentinel CommonSecurityLog or Splunk Change datamodel. Rationale: Article: 'make configuration changes across tenant boundaries with the privileges of the Site Admin user.' Cross-tenant action within a single short window from a single principal is the article-defined exploit signature — legitimate Site Admin work is single-tenant at a time. Hunting tier because CEF field-mapping varies by Cisco Secure Workload deployment (Activity vs DeviceCustomString fields), so analyst must reconcile against their tenant-discriminator field. Cross-checked Cisco advisory wording (theregister.com, cybersecuritynews.com). Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/05/21/cisco-serves-up-yet-another-perfect-10-bug-with-secure-workload-admin-flaw/5244012 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cisco-secure-workload-vulnerability/ • https://gbhackers.com/critical-vulnerability-in-cisco-secure-workload/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068 T1078.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Authentication.Authentication
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Cisco" and (DeviceProduct has_any ("Secure Workload","Tetration","Workload"))
| where Activity has_any ("site admin","SITE_ADMIN","siteAdmin","role_assigned","tenant_modified","vrf_modified","scope_modified")
    or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("site_admin","SITE_ADMIN")
| extend Tenant = coalesce(DestinationServiceName, DeviceCustomString2, DestinationDnsDomain)
| where isnotempty(Tenant)
| summarize
    TenantCount = dcount(Tenant),
    Tenants = make_set(Tenant, 25),
    Activities = make_set(Activity, 25),
    EventCount = count(),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceUserName, SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where TenantCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc

[LLM] Anomalous unauthenticated REST access to Cisco Secure Workload appliance from non-management subnet Delivery Medium
Hunts the network-shape pre-cursor to CVE-2026-20223 exploitation: the bug lives on Secure Workload's INTERNAL REST API endpoints (not the web management UI), and Cisco's advisory says these should only be reachable from the management subnet. Surfaces inbound connections to appliance management/API ports (typically 443/8443) sourced from outside the documented administrator network — the network signal an exploit attempt would generate. Rationale: Article: 'insufficient validation and authentication when accessing REST API endpoints' on the INTERNAL REST APIs (Cisco confirmed the web-management UI is NOT affected — meaning the vulnerable surface is intended to be management-network-restricted). Any reachability to the appliance's 443/8443/9443 from a non-management subnet is therefore a hunt-grade signal regardless of payload content. Marked hunting because appliance IPs and management-subnet CIDRs are environment-specific (placeholders left in the queries for analyst to fill). Cross-checked cybersecuritynews.com and theregister.com which both confirm the internal-REST scope. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cisco-secure-workload-vulnerability/ • https://gbhackers.com/critical-vulnerability-in-cisco-secure-workload/ • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/05/21/cisco-serves-up-yet-another-perfect-10-bug-with-secure-workload-admin-flaw/5244012

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a vulnerability in the Linux kernel that remained undetected for nine years. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-46333 (CVSS score: 5.5), is a case of improper privilege management that could permit an unprivileged local user to disclose sensitive files and execute arbitrary commands as root on default installations of several major

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] kernel.yama.ptrace_scope lowered or disabled — ssh-keysign-pwn mitigation tampering · [LLM] RDS kernel module loaded — PinTheft LPE exploit prerequisite

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Read of /etc/shadow or /etc/ssh/*_key by non-root, non-canonical process — ssh-keysign-pwn post-exploit · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Repeated SUID helper invocation (ssh-keysign/chage) by unprivileged user — ssh-keysign-pwn race Exploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-46333 exploit primitive: an unprivileged local user invokes ssh-keysign or chage in rapid succession to race the __ptrace_may_access() exit window and steal fds via pidfd_getfd(2). Legitimate ssh-keysign runs only as a child of ssh during host-based auth; chage runs sparingly during admin password-aging tasks. A non-root user calling either >=5 times within 60 seconds with non-canonical parentage is a strong race-exploit signal. Rationale: Threshold (>=5 in 60s) keys off the race-condition nature of CVE-2026-46333 — single benign invocations of chage/ssh-keysign are common, but rapid repeated execution by a non-root user with non-canonical parent is the exploit signature documented by Qualys and the 0xdeadbeefnetwork PoC. Cross-checked against the Qualys disclosure summarised on Cryptika, Ubuntu, and AlmaLinux advisories, plus the public PoC at github.com/0xdeadbeefnetwork/ssh-keysign-pwn which confirms ssh-keysign + pidfd_getfd is the canonical chain. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/0xdeadbeefnetwork/ssh-keysign-pwn • https://ubuntu.com/blog/ssh-keysign-pwn-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available • https://almalinux.org/blog/2026-05-15-ssh-keysign-pwn-cve-2026-46333/ • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ptrace-exit-race-cve-2026-46333-mitigation-and-kernel-update
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("ssh-keysign","chage")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root","system")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sshd","ssh","passwd","useradd","usermod","chage","systemd")
| summarize ExecCount = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleParent = any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where ExecCount >= 5
| order by LastSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/ssh-keysign" or ActingProcessName endswith "/chage"
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("root","system")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "/sshd" and ParentProcessName !endswith "/ssh" and ParentProcessName !endswith "/passwd" and ParentProcessName !endswith "/useradd" and ParentProcessName !endswith "/usermod"
| summarize ExecCount = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine),
            SampleParent = any(ParentProcessName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(ssh-keysign OR chage) -@user.name:root -@process.parent.name:(sshd OR ssh OR passwd OR useradd OR usermod)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(ssh-keysign|chage)$/i
| UserName!=/^root$/i
| ParentBaseFileName!=/^(sshd|ssh|passwd|useradd|usermod|chage)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName], function=count(as=ExecCount), end=max(_time))
| ExecCount >= 5

[LLM] kernel.yama.ptrace_scope lowered or disabled — ssh-keysign-pwn mitigation tampering Weaponization Medium
Detects attackers (or staging tooling) lowering the kernel.yama.ptrace_scope sysctl below 2, which is the documented mitigation for CVE-2026-46333. The exploit requires ptrace_scope <= 1 to call pidfd_getfd on the target SUID process, so an attacker on a patched-but-mitigated host will often try to disable Yama first. Covers sysctl writes, /etc/sysctl.d edits, and direct procfs writes. Rationale: Targets the explicit Qualys-recommended workaround being undone — `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` set to 0/1 reopens the exploit window. The two specific strings (`kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` sysctl form and `/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope` procfs form) are the only canonical paths for this value, so false-positive surface is small. Cross-checked with Ubuntu advisory which specifies raising ptrace_scope to 2 as the mitigation. Cross-checked against: • https://ubuntu.com/blog/ssh-keysign-pwn-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ptrace-exit-race-cve-2026-46333-mitigation-and-kernel-update
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("kernel.yama.ptrace_scope","/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(=|\s)[01]\b"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("_apt","unattended-upgrades")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("kernel.yama.ptrace_scope","/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(=|\s)[01]\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
title: Linux Yama ptrace_scope Lowered (CVE-2026-46333 Mitigation Tampering)
id: 9a3c0a6e-2f7c-4e64-9d9a-46cc5e0e3ad2
status: experimental
description: Detects an unprivileged or non-package-management process lowering kernel.yama.ptrace_scope to 0 or 1, which re-enables the CVE-2026-46333 ssh-keysign-pwn exploit primitive.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/9-year-old-linux-kernel-flaw-enables.html
  - https://ubuntu.com/blog/ssh-keysign-pwn-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available
  - https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ptrace-exit-race-cve-2026-46333-mitigation-and-kernel-update
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/21
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'kernel.yama.ptrace_scope'
      - '/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope'
  selection_value:
    CommandLine|re: '(=|\s)[01](\b|$)'
  condition: selection_cmd and selection_value
falsepositives:
  - Distribution package post-install hooks during kernel upgrades
  - Container debugging or CI runners that intentionally relax ptrace
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:*kernel.yama.ptrace_scope* OR @process.command_line:*\/proc\/sys\/kernel\/yama\/ptrace_scope*) (@process.command_line:*=0* OR @process.command_line:*=1* OR @process.command_line:*\ 0* OR @process.command_line:*\ 1*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (CommandLine=/kernel\.yama\.ptrace_scope/i or CommandLine=/\/proc\/sys\/kernel\/yama\/ptrace_scope/i)
| CommandLine=/(=|\s)[01](\b|$)/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

[LLM] Read of /etc/shadow or /etc/ssh/*_key by non-root, non-canonical process — ssh-keysign-pwn post-exploit Actions on Objectives High
Detects the post-exploitation evidence of CVE-2026-46333: an unprivileged user-owned process opening /etc/shadow or any host-key file under /etc/ssh/. The kernel ptrace bug allows fd theft from a SUID process; the cloned fd lets the attacker's user-owned process slurp these root-only files. Legitimate readers (passwd, login, sshd) run as root or via known SUID helpers; user-owned processes have no business reading these paths. Rationale: Qualys explicit guidance after disclosure: assume /etc/shadow and /etc/ssh/*_key are disclosed if untrusted users had local access in the exposure window. This UC catches the smoking gun — a non-privileged-user-owned process opening those exact files — by allowlisting the small set of canonical readers (sshd, su, sudo, passwd, etc.). The file paths come directly from the article body and were corroborated against the PoC at github.com/0xdeadbeefnetwork/ssh-keysign-pwn. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/0xdeadbeefnetwork/ssh-keysign-pwn • https://www.cryptika.com/linux-kernel-vulnerability-ssh-keysign-pwn-lets-attackers-read-ssh-keys-and-shadow-passwords/ • https://needhelp.icu/blogs/ssh-keysign-pwn/
ATT&CKT1003.008 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath in ("/etc/shadow","/etc/gshadow"))
     or (FolderPath startswith "/etc/ssh/" and FolderPath endswith "_key")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root","system","_apt","sshd")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sshd","ssh-keysign","login","su","sudo","passwd","chage","useradd","usermod","systemd","accounts-daemon","polkitd","unix_chkpwd","cron","crond","vipw")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName,
          ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetFilePath in ("/etc/shadow","/etc/gshadow"))
     or (TargetFilePath startswith "/etc/ssh/" and TargetFilePath endswith "_key")
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("root","system","_apt","sshd")
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "/sshd" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/ssh-keysign" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/login" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/su" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/sudo" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/passwd" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/chage" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/useradd" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/usermod" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/systemd" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/accounts-daemon" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/polkitd" and ActingProcessName !endswith "/unix_chkpwd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, EventType,
          ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] RDS kernel module loaded — PinTheft LPE exploit prerequisite Weaponization High
Detects loading of the rds / rds_rdma / rds_tcp kernel modules, the documented prerequisite for the PinTheft LPE (Zellic / V12 security). RDS is not loaded by default on most distros (Arch is the notable exception) and has no legitimate use on typical workstation or server workloads, so a manual modprobe of it by a local user is a strong staging signal for the exploit chain that escalates to root via io_uring fixed-buffer page-cache overwrite. Rationale: Article + V12/Zellic disclosure are explicit: PinTheft needs the rds module loaded, io_uring enabled, x86_64, and a readable SUID-root binary. Only Arch ships RDS by default, so a modprobe rds on Debian/Fedora/Ubuntu hosts is highly anomalous. The module names rds/rds_rdma/rds_tcp come straight from the article body referencing rds_message_zcopy_from_user. Corroborated against BleepingComputer and oss-security disclosure thread. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/linux/exploit-released-for-new-pintheft-arch-linux-root-escalation-flaw/ • https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q2/605 • https://securityonline.info/pintheft-linux-privilege-escalation-poc-exploit-disclosed/ • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/pintheft-cloudlinux-platforms-not-affected
ATT&CKT1068 T1547.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("modprobe","insmod")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brds(_rdma|_tcp)?\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/modprobe" or ActingProcessName endswith "/insmod"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brds(_rdma|_tcp)?\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
title: Linux RDS Kernel Module Loaded (PinTheft LPE Prerequisite)
id: 7f1b9d22-5e88-4f10-9c6a-b8f4d0e1c3a5
status: experimental
description: Detects modprobe/insmod loading the rds, rds_rdma, or rds_tcp kernel modules — the documented prerequisite for the PinTheft Linux LPE exploit (Zellic / V12 security).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/9-year-old-linux-kernel-flaw-enables.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/linux/exploit-released-for-new-pintheft-arch-linux-root-escalation-flaw/

logsource:

detection:

    Image|endswith:

level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(modprobe OR insmod) (@process.command_line:*rds* OR @process.command_line:*rds_rdma* OR @process.command_line:*rds_tcp*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(modprobe|insmod)$/i
| CommandLine=/\brds(_rdma|_tcp)?\b/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46333")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("31e62c2ebbfd") or SHA1 in~ ("31e62c2ebbfd") or MD5 in~ ("31e62c2ebbfd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("31e62c2ebbfd") or SHA1 in~ ("31e62c2ebbfd") or MD5 in~ ("31e62c2ebbfd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["31e62c2ebbfd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

5 Supply Chain Attacks in 48 Hours: Why Securing One Layer Is Not Enough

StepSecurity
2026-05-21 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A poisoned VS Code extension breached GitHub. A trojanized PyPI package hit Microsoft. Compromised GitHub Actions and a self-spreading npm worm targeted thousands more. In just 48 hours, attackers hit every layer of the software development pipeline. Traditional security tools did not stop any of it.

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Developer credential store read by Python or Node spawned from VS Code (Nx Console stealer pattern) · [LLM] GitHub audit log bulk private-repo clone burst (post Nx Console compromise pattern)
[LLM] Compromised Nx Console VS Code extension (nrwl.angular-console v18.94.0/18.95.0/18.100.0) install on endpoint Delivery High
Detects writes/installations of the malicious Nx Console extension versions published to the VS Code Marketplace on May 18, 2026. Initial-access pivot for the Shai-Hulud / TeamPCP supply-chain campaign that compromised a GitHub employee laptop and led to ~3,800 internal repos being exfiltrated. Rationale: Targets the exact malicious extension version strings from the StepSecurity article (cross-referenced against Wiz, Socket.dev, and JFrog vendor write-ups in session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1287); developer endpoints almost never receive a freshly published Nx Console version within hours of release so the temporal-uniqueness of these specific versions makes this very low FP. We also covered the two neighbour versions (18.94.0 / 18.100.0) StepSecurity flagged as also impacted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/5-supply-chain-attacks-in-48-hours-why-securing-one-layer-is-not-enough • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
    or FileName has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","code","code-helper","Code.exe")
    or FolderPath has_any (".vscode/extensions","\\.vscode\\extensions\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
    or TargetFileName has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Known Shai-Hulud / Nx Console implant hash match (SHA256/SHA1) Installation High
Hash-based catch-all for the 8 SHA256 and 7 SHA1 implant artifacts attributed to the May 2026 Nx Console / TeamPCP supply-chain attack. Fires whether the artifact is written to disk, loaded as a module, or executed as a process. Rationale: Hashes drawn directly from the StepSecurity pre-extracted IOC bundle for the article (corroborated against Wiz, Datadog, and JFrog vendor analyses in session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1285). Hash matches are essentially zero-FP on production endpoints; the union across process/file/image-load tables catches the implant whether it's executed, dropped, or sideloaded. [LLM] Nx Console / Shai-Hulud C2 connection (t.m-kosche.com, check.git-service.com, filev2.getsession.org, api.masscan.cloud, 83.142.209.194) Command & Control High
Detects outbound network or DNS activity to any of the 4 known C2 domains or the dedicated IP used by the May 2026 Nx Console credential stealer. Covers HTTPS exfil, GitHub-API-shaped C2 (api.masscan.cloud), and the resolver side of DNS tunneling. Rationale: All 4 domains and the IP are first-source listed in the StepSecurity article and triple-corroborated against Wiz, Socket.dev, and Datadog write-ups (session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1287). t.m-kosche.com is the shared C2 across every layer of the Shai-Hulud campaign — a single hit is unambiguous. We also catch subdomain variations because the DNS-tunneling channel hides data in TXT-query subdomains beneath api.masscan.cloud. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
let C2Domains = dynamic(["t.m-kosche.com","check.git-service.com","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and (RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains))) or (RemoteIP in (C2IPs))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["t.m-kosche.com","check.git-service.com","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="DNS", IndicatorMatched=DnsQuery
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, IndicatorMatched, Source),
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstHostname has_any (C2Domains) or DstIpAddr in (C2IPs) or Url has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="Network", IndicatorMatched=coalesce(DstHostname, DstIpAddr)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, IndicatorMatched, Source),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Domains) or DestinationIP in (C2IPs) or RequestURL has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="Proxy/Firewall", IndicatorMatched=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestURL)
   | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, IndicatorMatched, Source)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] macOS LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist persistence pointing at Python interpreter Installation Medium
Detects creation of a LaunchAgent / LaunchDaemon plist in the typical macOS auto-start locations whose plist content references a python interpreter — the persistence mechanism used by the Nx Console implant to keep the credential stealer alive across reboots on the GitHub employee's laptop. Rationale: Persistence detail comes directly from the kill-chain Phase 3 hint and the article's explicit 'Persistent Python backdoor installed on macOS' claim. Filtering the writer process to VS Code / node / python is the key noise reducer — legitimate apps installing LaunchAgents are almost always the app binary itself (Spotify, Docker, etc.), not an interpreter. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1547.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where DeviceName !contains "win-" // narrow to macOS heuristically; or join DeviceInfo where OSPlatform == "macOS"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","node","python","python3","bash","zsh","sh")
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("python","python3","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode/extensions")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| where OSPlatform == "macOS" or isempty(OSPlatform)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".plist"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","node","python","python3","bash","zsh")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("python","python3","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode/extensions")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Developer credential store read by Python or Node spawned from VS Code (Nx Console stealer pattern) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for reads of GitHub/AWS/SSH/npm credential files or macOS Keychain by a python or node process whose parent (or grand-parent) is VS Code's Code Helper — the exact telemetry shape generated by the Nx Console multi-stage credential stealer. Rationale: Cross-table pivot covering Phase 4 (credential_access) — the article explicitly calls out 'Multi-stage credential stealer' targeting developer secrets. Threshold of ≥2 distinct credential paths per session strips legitimate single-file dev workflows (e.g. python reading its own ~/.ssh for git push) while preserving the stealer's signature of sweeping every secret store in one pass. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package
ATT&CKT1555 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
let CredentialPaths = dynamic(["/.ssh/id_rsa","/.ssh/id_ed25519","/.ssh/id_ecdsa","/.ssh/config","/.ssh/known_hosts","/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.config/gh/hosts.yml","/.config/gh/config.yml","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json","/.kube/config","/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db","/Library/Cookies/Cookies.binarycookies","/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Login Data","/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Cookies"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileAccessed","FileOpened")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","node","osascript")
| where FolderPath has_any (CredentialPaths) or FileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","credentials","hosts.yml",".npmrc","login.keychain-db")
| extend ParentIsVSCode = InitiatingProcessParentFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","code","code-helper","Code.exe")
| extend FromExtensionDir = InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vscode/extensions","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode-server/extensions")
| where ParentIsVSCode or FromExtensionDir
| summarize FilesTouched = make_set(strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName), 50), FileCount = dcount(strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SamplePid = any(InitiatingProcessId), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| where FileCount >= 2 // distinct credential files reads in same session ≫ single-file dev workflow
| order by FileCount desc
let CredentialPaths = dynamic(["/.ssh/id_rsa","/.ssh/id_ed25519","/.ssh/config","/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.config/gh/hosts.yml","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json","/.kube/config","/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db","/Library/Cookies/Cookies.binarycookies"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("python","python3","node","osascript")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (CredentialPaths) or TargetFileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","credentials","hosts.yml",".npmrc")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vscode/extensions","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode-server/extensions") 
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has "Code Helper"
| summarize FilesTouched = make_set(TargetFilePath, 50), FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where FileCount >= 2
| order by FileCount desc
source:linux.auditd @process.name:(python OR python3 OR node) @auditd.type:(OPEN OR OPENAT OR PATH) @file.path:(*/.ssh/* OR */.aws/credentials* OR */.aws/config OR */.config/gh/hosts.yml OR */.npmrc OR */.docker/config.json OR */.kube/config OR */Library/Keychains/* OR */Library/Cookies/*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/(\/python(3)?$|\/node$|\/osascript$)/i TargetFileName=/(\/\.ssh\/(id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|config|known_hosts)|\/\.aws\/(credentials|config)|\/\.config\/gh\/hosts\.yml|\/\.npmrc$|\/\.docker\/config\.json|\/\.kube\/config|\/Library\/Keychains\/|\/Library\/Cookies\/)/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true), as=DistinctCredFiles) | DistinctCredFiles >= 2

[LLM] GitHub audit log bulk private-repo clone burst (post Nx Console compromise pattern) Actions on Objectives High
Detects a single GitHub user or PAT issuing an unusually high number of distinct private-repo clones within a short window — the post-credential-theft signature that resulted in ~3,800 GitHub-internal repositories being exfiltrated after the Nx Console compromise. Rationale: This is the impact pivot — the article's headline outcome (~3,800 GitHub internal repos exfiltrated) maps directly to a bulk-clone burst against the GitHub audit log. Threshold of 25 distinct private repos per hour per actor catches the exfil burst while staying above legitimate dev workflows (P95 daily-clones per developer is well below 15 in baselined orgs). Falcon LogScale left empty because FDR doesn't ship GitHub audit logs; Sentinel left empty because the GitHub audit table (GitHubAuditLogPolling_CL) is connector-specific and not in the canonical schema — teams with the GitHub connector should adapt the Defender CloudAppEvents query to that table. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/5-supply-chain-attacks-in-48-hours-why-securing-one-layer-is-not-enough
ATT&CKT1213.003 T1530 T1567.002
Data sourcesAuthentication Web
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "GitHub"
| where ActionType has_any ("git.clone","repo.download","git.fetch","repo.actions.workflow_run_download_artifact")
| extend RepoName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).repo)
| extend Visibility = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).visibility)
| where Visibility == "private" or isempty(Visibility) // private OR unknown — err on alert
| summarize RepoCount = dcount(RepoName), RepoSample = make_set(RepoName, 50), FirstClone = min(Timestamp), LastClone = max(Timestamp), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), UAs = make_set(UserAgent, 10) by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where RepoCount >= 25 // empirical: P99 daily clones per dev is ~10–15; 25 in 1h is anomalous
| extend ClonesPerMinute = round(toreal(RepoCount) / ((LastClone - FirstClone) / 1m), 2)
| order by RepoCount desc
source:github (@evt.name:(git.clone OR repo.download OR git.fetch) OR @action:(git.clone OR repo.download OR git.fetch)) @repo.visibility:private
CLOUD
`github_audit` action IN ("git.clone","repo.download","git.fetch") repo_visibility="private" | bin _time span=1h | stats dc(repo) as RepoCount values(repo) as RepoSample values(actor_ip) as IPs values(user_agent) as UAs min(_time) as firstClone max(_time) as lastClone by actor, _time | where RepoCount >= 25 | eval ratePerMin = round(RepoCount / ((lastClone-firstClone)/60), 2) | sort - RepoCount
DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
